messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia, a 31-year-old married dancer of Oceania heritage, came to treatment after years of carrying a childhood memory she had learned to keep hidden. As a girl, she had witnessed her father attack her mother in their home while relatives were present and did nothing; the betrayal of that scene stayed with her less as a single image than as a shattered understanding of safety. In her present life, small things can still cut straight through her day: hearing a name that sounds like her father’s or another man from that time can make her feel immediately on edge, and if she notices the sensation of her own heart pounding, she is suddenly back inside that old fear. In those moments she does not simply feel alarmed; she is struck by the sense that people cannot be trusted, that she was betrayed by someone who should have protected her, and that there must have been something about her that made it happen. She has come to believe that being watched is dangerous because watching, for her, once meant violence going unnoticed. Once those reminders hit, they do not just frighten her; they quickly settle into the thought that the world is still the kind of place where danger is hidden in plain sight and other people cannot be relied on. A glance, a name, or the feel of her own racing pulse would seem to confirm for her that she has no reason to expect safety from anyone around her.

When Malia tries to remember the event, the memory does not come to her in a steady, narratable way. At times she can call it to mind and feels a flood of intense shame, as though she is the one who should have prevented what happened, even though she was only a child. After those images surfaced, even small things around her — a man’s voice in the hallway, a name that sounded like her father’s, the abrupt scrape of a chair — began to feel like fresh reminders of the same danger. The memory had taught her body to treat those details as signals that the past might be starting again. At other times she can describe the outline of it with a strange numbness, as if it happened to someone else in another family, and she hates that blank distance because it makes the whole thing feel unreal and yet no less true. Each time the memory returned like that, she caught herself thinking that there must be something permanently wrong with her for it still to intrude so vividly and yet feel so far away. The recollection seemed to hand her the explanation that she had somehow been marked by it, and that thought settled into a harsh, shame-filled view of herself. What unsettles her most is how unexpectedly it arrives: something in the environment can bring the scene back in full without warning, and once it does, the old conclusions about herself and other people harden again. She is left certain that trust is foolish, that the people closest to you can turn, and that her own presence somehow failed to protect the people she loved. That certainty then made ordinary life newly suspicious to her, so that almost any unclear tone, familiar-sounding name, or sharp movement could start to feel like a warning sign. Because she was already expecting betrayal, she began to notice and cling to those cues far more quickly than she had before. Those recollections are not passive memories for Malia; they press directly into the beliefs she already fears are true.

Over the years, those beliefs have fed back into how she responds to the world around her. As a dancer, Malia spends her days in studios with mirrors, instructors giving corrections, and audiences or casting directors watching her body from the outside, and being observed can feel unnervingly close to the kind of attention that once preceded humiliation at home. A glance from a teacher, a pause before feedback, or the sense that someone is studying her closely can trigger the old conviction that others are not what they seem and that scrutiny means something bad is coming. Then she finds herself listening for names, for tones, for any hint of recognition that might signal danger, and even the pounding of her heart becomes proof that the threat is real. When that happens, the shame from her memory returns with it, and she becomes even more certain that there is something about her that brought all this on. The loop has narrowed her world: she has started holding back in rehearsal, feeling less able to relax in the studio, and she is more guarded with colleagues than she used to be, especially when she senses eyes on her.

Malia’s marriage has also been affected in quieter ways. Her husband has noticed that she sometimes goes still when he says a name that resembles one from her childhood, or when his attention lands on her after an argument and she suddenly looks as though she wants to disappear. She does not tell him that these moments make her feel watched and cornered, because part of her fears that once she speaks it aloud, he too might prove untrustworthy. Instead she keeps the old shame private, hoping that if she can manage the reactions herself, she will not need to admit how much the memory still governs her. But the more she tries to outrun those moments, the more sensitized she becomes to them; hearing a related name or feeling her heart race now has enough power to bring back the whole memory, and the memory in turn drags her back into the same judgments about betrayal, fault, and hidden threat.

She finally sought help after a rehearsal in which a director called out a name similar to her father’s and she felt her heart slam so hard she had to leave the room. Standing outside the studio, shaken and ashamed, Malia realized that she was no longer sure she could keep living around these sudden returns of the past. What she fears most is that she will always feel watched, always assume betrayal, and never be able to trust either other people or her own body again; what she hopes for is to remember without being overwhelmed by shame, and to move through her marriage and work without every passing name, glance, or racing heartbeat pulling her back into that childhood scene.
